```{r setup, include=FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(echo = TRUE, message = FALSE, warning = FALSE,

}
if (!requireNamespace("ggplot2", quietly = TRUE)) {

}
library(ggplot2)
set.seed(42)
```

## Goal

Split a mock retail customer base into groups with distinct behaviours, explain
what distinguishes them, and use their estimated response propensity to target a
promotional campaign. The simulated customers are drawn from five hidden
personas; those labels are used only to evaluate clustering, never as model
inputs.

## 1. Data overview

```{r data}
customers <- load_customers()
dim(customers)
head(customers)
summary(customers[c("age", "income_k", "tenure_months", "recency_days",
                    "frequency_12m", "monetary_12m", "nps_score")])
```

Each row is one customer. Campaign response and subsequent six-month churn are
binary outcomes. The persona label is retained for validation.

```{r overview}
persona_summary <- aggregate(
  cbind(frequency_12m, monetary_12m, recency_days, responded_campaign,
        churned_6m) ~ true_persona,
  data = customers, FUN = mean
)
persona_summary
```

## 2. Baseline: RFM segmentation

Recency, frequency, and monetary value are independently scored from 1 to 5.
The recency score is reversed so 5 means a more recent purchase.

```{r rfm}
rfm <- rfm_scores(customers)
customers <- cbind(customers, rfm)
as.data.frame(table(customers$rfm_segment))
```

RFM is transparent, but it omits channel engagement, discount preference, and
other behavioural differences.

## 3. Behavioural clustering

The clustering inputs describe what customers do, not their demographics.
Right-skewed measures are transformed with `log1p`; all eight inputs are then
standardised.

```{r transform}
x <- cluster_preprocessor(customers)
dim(x)
```

### Choosing the number of segments

The elbow, silhouette, bootstrap stability (mean pairwise adjusted Rand index),
and Gaussian-mixture BIC give complementary views of candidate values of *k*.
Silhouette is calculated on a reproducible sample to keep the distance
calculation practical for the full customer set.

```{r select-k, cache=TRUE}
k_range <- 2:10
k_scores <- evaluate_k(x, k_range)
stability <- stability_by_k(x, k_range, n_boot = 10, frac = 0.8)
bic <- gmm_bic(x, k_range)
selection <- data.frame(
  k = k_range,
  inertia = k_scores$inertia,
  silhouette = k_scores$silhouette,
  stability = unname(stability),
  gmm_bic = unname(bic)
)
selection
```

```{r selection-plot}
selection_long <- rbind(
  data.frame(k = k_range, measure = "Silhouette", value = selection$silhouette),
  data.frame(k = k_range, measure = "Bootstrap stability", value = selection$stability)
)
ggplot(selection_long, aes(k, value)) +
  geom_line(colour = "#2a78d6") + geom_point(colour = "#2a78d6") +
  facet_wrap(~measure, scales = "free_y") +
  labs(title = "Cluster separation and reproducibility", x = "Number of clusters (k)",
       y = "Score") +
  theme_minimal()
```

The elbow and GMM BIC have different scales, so they are reported as tables
rather than combined on one axis. The example proceeds with five segments, the
known number of simulated personas.

### Compare clustering algorithms

```{r compare, cache=TRUE}
k <- 5
comparison <- compare_algorithms(x, k, truth = customers$true_persona)
comparison$scores
customers$cluster <- comparison$labels[["K-Means"]]
```

### Segment profiles and names

Business archetypes encode expected high/low directions for a handful of
profile features. The Hungarian assignment matches each cluster to at most one
archetype.

```{r profiles}
profile <- index_vs_average(customers, "cluster", PROFILE_FEATURES)
segment_names <- name_segments(profile)
customers$segment <- unname(segment_names[as.character(customers$cluster)])
profile_named <- data.frame(
  cluster = rownames(profile),
  segment = unname(segment_names[rownames(profile)]),
  profile,
  row.names = NULL,
  check.names = FALSE
)
profile_named
```

```{r profile-heatmap, fig.height=6}
profile_long <- data.frame(
  cluster = rep(rownames(profile), times = ncol(profile)),
  feature = rep(colnames(profile), each = nrow(profile)),
  z_score = as.vector(profile)
)
profile_long$segment <- segment_names[profile_long$cluster]
ggplot(profile_long, aes(feature, segment, fill = z_score)) +
  geom_tile() +
  scale_fill_gradient2(low = "#184f95", mid = "#f0efec", high = "#b52f2f") +
  labs(title = "Segment profile relative to the customer average",
       x = NULL, y = NULL, fill = "z-score") +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 40, hjust = 1))
```

### Segment map and validation

```{r pca, fig.height=4}
pc <- stats::prcomp(x, center = FALSE, scale. = FALSE)
map <- data.frame(PC1 = pc$x[, 1], PC2 = pc$x[, 2],
                  segment = customers$segment)
ggplot(map, aes(PC1, PC2, colour = segment)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.45, size = 0.8) +
  labs(title = "Customer segments projected onto the first two PCs",
       colour = "Segment") +
  theme_minimal()
```

```{r validation}
persona_by_segment <- prop.table(table(customers$true_persona, customers$segment), 1)
round(persona_by_segment, 2)

rfm_by_segment <- prop.table(table(customers$rfm_segment, customers$segment), 2)
round(rfm_by_segment, 2)

adjusted_rand(customers$true_persona, customers$cluster)
```

The persona cross-tabulation measures recovery of the simulated source groups.
The RFM cross-tabulation shows how behavioural groups cut across a simpler
rule-based segmentation.

## 4. Explain segments with a random forest

This supervised model predicts the already-assigned behavioural segment from
all customer attributes. A held-out classification report measures how well a
future customer can be assigned, while permutation importance indicates which
attributes help distinguish the segments.

```{r explain, cache=TRUE}
segment_fit <- train_segment_classifier(customers)
segment_fit$report
head(segment_fit$importance, 15)
```

## 5. Campaign response modelling

Compare a logistic-regression baseline with gradient boosting on a stratified
30% hold-out set. Both models include segment membership as a predictor.

```{r response, cache=TRUE}
response_fit <- train_response_models(customers)
auc <- vapply(response_fit$results, `[[`, numeric(1), "auc")
auc
```

```{r roc}
roc_data <- do.call(rbind, lapply(names(response_fit$results), function(name) {
  result <- response_fit$results[[name]]
  data.frame(fpr = result$fpr, tpr = result$tpr, model = name)
}))
ggplot(roc_data, aes(fpr, tpr, colour = model)) +
  geom_line() +
  geom_abline(slope = 1, intercept = 0, linetype = "dashed", colour = "grey50") +
  coord_equal() +
  labs(title = "Campaign response ROC curves", x = "False positive rate",
       y = "True positive rate", colour = "Model") +
  theme_minimal()
```

Decile lift ranks customers by the selected model's predicted probability.

```{r gains}
best_name <- names(auc)[which.max(auc)]
best_scores <- response_fit$results[[best_name]]$scores
gains <- gains_table(response_fit$y_test, best_scores)
best_name
gains
```

## 6. Marketing playbook

```{r playbook}
response_predictions <- predict_response(response_fit, customers)
customers$p_response <- response_predictions[[best_name]]

actions <- c(
  "Loyal High-Value" = "VIP / loyalty tier, early access, and referrals; protect margin",
  "Bargain Hunters" = "Targeted promo codes and bundles; cap discount depth",
  "Digital Natives" = "App push and social campaigns; use mobile-first offers",
  "Occasional Big Spenders" = "Personalised premium recommendations around purchase cycles",
  "At-Risk Lapsed" = "Low-cost win-back sequence; suppress costly channels if inactive"
)
playbook <- aggregate(
  cbind(monetary_12m, responded_campaign, p_response, churned_6m) ~ segment,
  data = customers, FUN = mean
)
counts <- as.data.frame(table(customers$segment), stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
names(counts) <- c("segment", "customers")
revenue <- aggregate(monetary_12m ~ segment, customers, sum)
names(revenue)[[2]] <- "revenue"
playbook <- merge(playbook, counts, by = "segment")
playbook <- merge(playbook, revenue, by = "segment")
playbook$revenue_share <- playbook$revenue / sum(playbook$revenue)
playbook$action <- unname(actions[playbook$segment])
playbook[order(-playbook$revenue_share), ]
```

```{r export}
output <- customers[c("customer_id", "segment", "rfm_segment", "R", "F", "M",
                      "p_response")]
dir.create(file.path("data", "processed"), recursive = TRUE, showWarnings = FALSE)
utils::write.csv(output, file.path("data", "processed", "customer_segments.csv"),
                 row.names = FALSE)
message("Saved ", nrow(output), " scored customers to data/processed/customer_segments.csv")
```

## Interpretation

Use the resulting cluster scores, profiles, and hold-out metrics to decide
whether the simulated groups are useful. For real customer data, validate
stability over time, test segment-specific offers, and prefer uplift modelling
when the goal is to estimate incremental campaign impact.
